title: MB9-27240
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellant is appealing the RPD's decision.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of India. He is alleging that he fears returning to his country because he is afraid that the police will go after him again. On XXXX XXXX, 2009, the appellant allegedly married a woman who was in a relationship with another man. His wife supposedly returned to live with her family. The police apparently sided with his wife's uncle to get him to pay money for a divorce. The appellant's family allegedly paid for his divorce and the police tortured his father. The police and his wife's uncle reportedly falsely accused the appellant of helping activists, thereby attributing a political opinion to him. The police apparently arrested and tortured the appellant twice. Once released, the appellant reportedly fled to Switzerland before coming to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2013.

The representative of the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship intervened in this case, asking the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) to reject the appellant's refugee protection claim because of the credibility issues noted in his written account. He pointed out the appellant's delay in seeking Canada's protection, which demonstrates a lack of subjective fear.

On November 1, 2019, the RPD rejected the appellant's refugee protection claim, finding that he was not a credible witness because of contradictions in his testimony and behaviour, which demonstrates a lack of subjective fear in India.

The appellant is appealing the RPD's decision. He is arguing that the RPD failed to analyze his refugee protection claim under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA). The appellant is also arguing that the RPD breached the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness by disregarding much of the evidence that he presented. The appellant is also alleging that the RPD erred in its assessment of his credibility since the contradictions identified are minor and his delay in claiming refugee protection is not a determinative factor. In addition, the appellant is also arguing that the RPD erred in failing to analyze an internal flight alternative (IFA).

In my view, the determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD breached the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness and whether it erred in its assessment of the appellant's credibility. After conducting a complete and independent analysis of the evidence presented, I conclude that the RPD decision was incorrect.
The appeal is allowed. I refer the matter to a differently constituted RPD panel.

The RAD must apply the standard of correctness in accordance with the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Huruglica.2 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing credibility.3 In my view, the RPD did not enjoy any particular advantage in this case.
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: As a result, I will conduct my own analysis of the record, which includes listening to the recording of the hearing, to establish whether the RPD erred, applying the correctness standard of review. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL Analysis of the refugee protection claim under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act
The appellant is arguing that the RPD failed to analyze his refugee protection claim under section 96 of the IRPA.4

I am sensitive to the fact that, as the appellant points out in his appeal memorandum, although a negative credibility finding may be determinative in the case of a refugee protection claim under section 96 of the IRPA, that is not necessarily so in the case of a refugee protection claim under section 97. That said, with all due respect to the appellant, I am of the opinion that, in this case, this criticism is unfounded for the following reasons.

First, the RPD clearly states at the outset of its decision that the refugee protection claim concerns an alleged fear of persecution based on an imputed political opinion. Second, the RPD rejected the appellant's refugee protection claim essentially because it found that he was not a credible witness and it did not believe the events alleged by the appellant. In these circumstances, it seems to me that such a conclusion applies to both an analysis under section 96 of the IRPA and an analysis under section 97. Ultimately, the RPD concluded that the appellant is neither a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA nor a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1).
In light of the foregoing, I am of the opinion that the RPD did indeed analyze the appellant's refugee protection claim under section 96 of the IRPA. Natural justice
The appellant alleges that the RPD breached the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness by disregarding much of the evidence that he presented.

Although the RPD did not refer to or discuss all of the evidence in its reasons for decision, it is generally understood that the more relevant the evidence, the more important it is to mention it in the reasons.5 Moreover, there must be a sound and articulated reason for dismissing a refugee protection claimant's evidence as self-serving.

In this case, the appellant submitted several pieces of personal evidence in support of his claims, namely, exhibits C-4 to C-7. These consist of affidavits from his brother, a friend, his father and a sarpanch. The RPD's comments come down to the RPD not giving any probative value to the documents submitted, with the exception of Exhibit C-6, his father's affidavit, because there are inconsistencies in each of the documents and because the RPD considered them to be self-serving.

In my view, it is not clear from these comments exactly how the documents were unsatisfactory, what inconsistencies were noted by the RPD, or what the appellant's explanations were for those inconsistencies. In fact, the recording of the hearing reveals that the RPD did not question the appellant about this evidence. Consequently, the RPD's decision does not mention that it obtained and assessed the appellant's responses to determine whether or not his explanations for the inconsistencies noted were satisfactory. This should have been done, as this evidence directly relates to the main allegations of the appellant's refugee protection claim.

In light of the foregoing, I conclude that the RPD did indeed err significantly in disregarding this evidence without providing sufficient reasons. It is impossible for me to remedy this error by confirming, setting aside its determination and substituting a determination that, in my opinion, should have been made without holding an oral hearing in order to re-examine the evidence, particularly exhibits C-4 to C-7 that were presented to the RPD, including the appellant's testimony.
Consequently, I refer the matter to a differently constituted RPD panel for re-determination. The appellant's other criticisms

As for the appellant's claims that the RPD considered minor contradictions and his delay in claiming refugee protection in Canada to find that he was not credible, I do not consider that I need to address this on appeal, given my earlier conclusion regarding natural justice. The differently constituted panel will be able to assess the appellant's credibility.

In closing, with respect to the appellant's claim on appeal that the RPD erred in failing to analyze an IFA, suffice it to say that it was not necessary for the RPD to do so because it did not find the appellant credible with respect to the allegations forming the basis of his refugee protection claim.

The appeal is allowed. I refer the matter to a differently constituted RPD panel.
